desc:
An array nums is convex if its consecutive differences never decrease: nums[i + 1] - nums[i] ≤ nums[i + 2] - nums[i + 1] for every valid i. Such an array may fall, then stay flat, then rise (any of the three phases may be empty), and flat stretches can occur only at the bottom.

Return the smallest value in nums using O(log n) comparisons.

For example, [10, 6, 3, 1, 0, 0, 1, 3] is convex (differences -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2) and its minimum is 0.
constraints: nums[i + 1] - nums[i] ≤ nums[i + 2] - nums[i + 1] for every valid i
hints: Look at the differences d[i] = nums[i + 1] - nums[i]. What does convexity say about the sequence d?
d is sorted in non-decreasing order, so the sign of d[i] flips at most once: from negative to non-negative. The array keeps falling while d[i] < 0.
Binary search the first index i with nums[i + 1] - nums[i] ≥ 0 (treat i = n - 1 as true). Then nums[i] is the minimum.
editorial: Convexity makes the sequence of differences sorted. Before the first non-negative difference the array strictly falls; from that point on it never falls again. So the minimum is at the first index i whose difference to the right is ≥ 0 (or at the last index if there is none).

The predicate 'nums[i + 1] - nums[i] ≥ 0' is therefore monotone (false...false, true...true) and is searched with a standard lower-bound binary search over [0, n - 1], where the last index counts as true. Flat stretches do no harm: they have difference 0, which is true, and because differences cannot decrease afterwards they can only sit at the minimum level.

This is the discrete form of finding the minimum of a convex function by checking the slope. It takes O(log n) time and O(1) space. Plain unimodal arrays that are not convex can contain flat steps elsewhere, which would break this argument, so the convexity guarantee matters.
